bib.title: Chapter 4. Adding Knowledge: Syncopation (Generative AI Design Patterns)

question: How can a basic RAG pipeline be extended so it retrieves better, ranks and cleans retrieved chunks, earns user trust, and handles complex multi-hop questions?
contributions: Pattern 9 Index-Aware Retrieval (hypothetical answers/HyDE, query expansion, hybrid search, GraphRAG)
Pattern 10 Node Postprocessing (reranking, hybrid fusion, query expansion/decomposition, obsolete filtering, contextual compression, disambiguation, personalization)
Pattern 11 Trustworthy Generation (out-of-domain detection, citations, guardrails, observability, human feedback, CRAG, Self-RAG, UI)
Pattern 12 Deep Search (iterative retrieve-think-generate loop; deep research as a variant)

limits: Every worked example is a single illustrative query on one corpus (Alexander history book, geology textbooks, Bach articles, Wikipedia); no benchmark, metric, baseline comparison, or repeat runs. Nothing is measured.

Hallucinated, obsolete or irrelevant content in HyDE/query expansion is conceded to risk losing RAG's grounding (Pattern 9 Considerations); query expansion may change user intent; GraphRAG may bring conflicting or old document versions.

HyDE benefit is conditioned on the LLM already knowing the domain; the chapter says it works for fine details only 'in a domain (such as well-known history) in which the foundational model can generate a plausible answer'.
Thresholds (out-of-domain, relevance) are domain-specific and need continuing tuning; strict guardrails lose information; human verification does not scale (Pattern 11 Limitations).
The trust-from-observability claim, the 'rerankers are much more accurate than embedding models' claim, and the 'six months old' freshness example have no cited evidence.

Several code listings are truncated in the PDF (long lines cut), e.g. the hybrid alpha value and KnowledgeGraphRAGRetriever args. Pattern 11 Considerations call Self-RAG a prompt-based reflection scheme, whereas Asai et al. is a fine-tuned model with reflection tokens.
Chapter text refers to 'Node Preprocessing' once where Node Postprocessing is meant. Some products named (BGE reranker via Pinecone, Perplexity, NotebookLM, node-DeepResearch) will have dated.
practices: Treat HyDE, query expansion, hybrid search and GraphRAG as separate options to test per content type and question type, not a bundle (Pattern 9 Solution).
Use HyDE when the answer involves logic or fine details in a domain the LLM knows; HyDE can also generate one hypothetical answer per perspective and restrict RAG to matching documents (Pattern 9).
Use query expansion when users write non-technical language over a technical knowledge base, and to disambiguate (Pattern 9).
When hybrid search is unsupported by the vector store, run two retrievers, merge, and pass the merged list to a reranker, then take top-K by relevance score (Pattern 10).
Rerank with an LLM or a fine-tuned reranker like BGE since an embedding must compress a chunk into one vector (Pattern 10).
Filter obsolete chunks by metadata (e.g., keep latest publication year) rather than pairwise LLM conflict checks (Pattern 10).
Fold contextual compression, disambiguation and relevance scoring into one structured-output call to limit LLM calls (Pattern 10).
Check disambiguation against the first chunk only: N-1 calls (Pattern 10).
Add conversation summary and user history in postprocessing for personalization (Pattern 10).
Short-circuit retrieval and generation for out-of-domain queries using embedding distance, zero-shot classification, keyword requirements, or a weighted mix (Pattern 11).

Citations are the most effective trust measure; use a classifier to find claims needing citation, look them up in the store, and mark claims with no source such as '[Citation needed]' (Pattern 11 Example).
Apply guardrails before retrieval, after retrieval, before generation and after generation, and on failure rewrite the query and regenerate (Pattern 11).

Use CRAG to evaluate retrieved chunks and fall back to web or enterprise search or decompose-then-recompose; use Self-RAG for self-evaluation, adaptive retrieval and controlled generation (Pattern 11).
Maintain state across Deep Search iterations, start from a simple question, fill gaps iteratively, parallelise subqueries, and cap budget (Pattern 12).
Evaluate Deep Search with an open-source framework such as Ragas, with a weighted score over relevance, comprehensiveness, accuracy, coherence, citation quality, efficiency (Pattern 12).

terms.definition: hypothetical document embedding: match chunks to an LLM-generated hypothetical answer instead of the question
use an LLM to add context and translate query terms to those used in the chunks
having found a chunk with a partial answer, retrieve related chunks via graph relationships; the document store is a graph database
inserts a step between retrieval and generation to increase relevance, reduce ambiguity, and handle content updates and personalization
reduce a retrieved chunk to only the text relevant to the query
corrective RAG: an evaluator scores retrieved chunks and triggers web/enterprise search or decompose-then-recompose
reflection in RAG: self-evaluation, adaptive retrieval, controlled generation
metadata tracked through the attention mechanism to attribute every generated token to sources
iterative process of searching, reading and reasoning with a thinking step and external tools
variation of Deep Search that outputs a long-form report of answers to the original and follow-up questions
